reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities
chapter_title: LRFD Design Requirements and Limit States for Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Design of laterally loaded deep foundations must address all applicable Limit States with appropriate load combinations, load factors and resistance factors, and requires interdisciplinary coordination between the structural and geotechnical engineers, especially in setting the LRFD design requirements.
sections.body: The design of laterally loaded deep foundations must address all applicable Limit States using appropriate load combinations, load factors and resistance factors. It requires interdisciplinary coordination between the structural engineer and the geotechnical engineer, especially for determining the LRFD design requirements for laterally loaded deep foundations. (p. 39)
key_points: Address all applicable Limit States with load combinations, load factors and resistance factors (p. 39).
Structural and geotechnical engineers coordinate on the LRFD requirements (p. 39).
sections.applicability: LRFD design framework for laterally loaded driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, and CFA piles

sections.title: Load Combinations and Load Factors
sections.summary: AASHTO (2014) Limit States: Strength, Service, Extreme Event and Fatigue; Strength I and IV, Extreme Event I and II and Service I typically govern foundations. Figures 4-1 to 4-5 show loads on abutments, piers, noise walls and slope stabilization; cap reactions from structural analysis, iterated with the geotechnical analysis, are the factored axial, lateral and moment effects; vary permanent load factors between maximum and minimum.
sections.body: LRFD requires identifying all potential failure modes, or Limit States; a Limit State is a condition in which some component does not fulfill its design function. AASHTO 2014 identifies four: Strength, Service, Extreme Events and Fatigue. Strength I, Strength IV, Extreme Events I and II and Service I typically govern deep foundation design; Service II, III and IV and Fatigue I and II are typically associated with the superstructure and not generally applicable to foundations (printed "not generally not applicable"). The total factored load for a Limit State is the sum of the load effects with their load factors and load modifiers; loads, combinations and factors are in AASHTO 2014. Figures 4-1 to 4-3 simplify typical loads: Figure 4-1 a bridge abutment in the longitudinal direction (transverse loads not shown); Figure 4-2 piers, with superstructure dead and live loads, wind on structure, wind on live load and temperature forces, and on the pier self-weight, wind on substructure, stream flow, buoyancy, ice flows, creep, shrinkage and other loads; in a river, stream or navigable waterway the foundations must be designed for scour, stream flow effects, water temperature effects and potentially vessel collision; Figure 4-3 horizontal forces and moments on noise walls. For landslide or slope stabilization the soil behind the elements can generate very high lateral forces (Figure 4-4); computing these loads is more complex than for retaining structures (Chapter 10). As in Figure 4-5 (p. 40), the reactions at the column-foundation joint or pile cap from the structural analysis are the force effects on the foundation, resolved into vertical, horizontal and moment components taken as the factored axial, lateral and moment effects at the top of the foundation or cap. Multiple iterations are typically performed to agree deformations and forces at the structure/foundation interface between the structural and geotechnical analyses. The resulting factored force effects are "substituted into Equation 4-1" (as printed; the chapter prints no Equation 4-1). Load factors for permanent loads have maximum and minimum values, so the structure is modeled with varied load factors to find the combination giving the maximum force effect on the foundation for the Limit State checks. Loads in Figures 4-1 to 4-5: permanent, CR creep, DD downdrag, DC dead load of structural components and nonstructural attachments, DW wearing surfaces and utilities, EH horizontal earth pressure, EL locked-in construction force effects, ES earth surcharge, EV vertical pressure from earth fill, PS secondary post-tensioning forces (Strength) or total prestress (Service), SH shrinkage; transient, BL blast, BR braking, CE centrifugal, CT vehicular collision, CV vessel collision, EQ earthquake, FR friction, IC ice, IM dynamic load allowance, LL live load, LS live load surcharge, PL pedestrian live load, SE settlement, TG temperature gradient, TU uniform temperature, WA water load and stream pressure, WL wind on live load, WS wind on structure. (pp. 39 to 43)
key_points: Strength I and IV, Extreme Event I and II and Service I typically govern foundations (p. 39).
Loads, combinations and factors are taken from AASHTO 2014 (p. 39).
Slope stabilization loads are very high and harder to compute than wall loads (p. 39).
Cap reactions are the factored axial, lateral and moment effects; iterate with the geotechnical analysis (p. 40).
Vary permanent load factors between maximum and minimum to find the governing effect (p. 40).

sections.title: Strength Limit State for Laterally Loaded Foundations
sections.summary: Strength Limit States cover geotechnical (soil failure) and structural (element failure, Chapter 11) strength. Resistance factors are not calibrated for lateral analysis; Table 4-1 (engineering judgment, Brown et al. 2010) for p-y analyses of driven piles or drilled shafts: 0.67 for a single element or single row with free head, 0.80 for an element in a multiple-row group with moment connection to the cap.
sections.body: Strength Limit State failure modes relate to strength and stability of the foundation under loads during the design life, evaluating geotechnical and structural resistances with an adequate margin against damage or collapse. For laterally loaded deep foundations they include geotechnical strength (failure of the soil) and structural strength (failure of the element; Chapter 11). Resistance factors have not been calibrated for lateral analysis; Table 4-1 gives recommended values for geotechnical strength limit state design, suggested from engineering judgment (Brown et al. 2010), as a check for ductility and geotechnical stability exceeding the reliability of the AASHTO (2014) provisions. They apply to lateral analysis of driven piles or drilled shafts for the Strength Limit State using load-displacement (p-y) analyses. Table 4-1, resistance factor phi_r (p. 44): pushover of an individual element, head free to rotate, 0.67; pushover of a single row of elements, retaining wall or abutment, head free to rotate, 0.67; pushover of an element within a multiple-row group with moment connection to the cap, 0.80. Practice is evolving: local DOTs have developed locally calibrated resistance factors from substantial successful experience and load tests (Abu-Hejleh et al. 2011); see also the Idaho Transportation Department Bridge Design LRFD Manual (2008), Robinson et al. (2006) for NCDOT and Boeckmann et al. (2014) for MoDOT. (pp. 43 to 44)
key_points: Strength Limit States: geotechnical (soil failure) and structural (element failure) (p. 43).
Resistance factors for lateral analysis are not calibrated; Table 4-1 is engineering judgment (p. 43).
phi_r 0.67: individual element or single row, wall or abutment, head free to rotate (p. 44).
phi_r 0.80: element in a multiple-row group with moment connection to the cap (p. 44).
Apply to p-y (load-displacement) analyses of driven piles or drilled shafts (p. 43).
Some DOTs have locally calibrated resistance factors (Abu-Hejleh et al. 2011) (p. 44).

sections.title: Service Limit State for Lateral Displacements
sections.summary: Service Limit States limit lateral displacement in interaction with the structure; the tolerable value is set by the structural engineer (joint closure, lean, rotation, contact, aesthetics) and is often less than the element can withstand. Load and resistance factors are 1.0; p-y analysis is recommended. Check head movement and rotation, movement under design-flood scour and at the superstructure.
sections.body: Service Limit State failure modes relate to performance problems such as deformation under regular operating conditions; for laterally loaded deep foundations they concern lateral displacement considering interaction with the structure. Foundations must have adequate structural and geotechnical resistance to keep displacements within tolerable levels, which are project specific and set by the project structural engineer (printed "tolerable lateral settlement"). A resistance factor of 1.0 applies; soil-structure interaction methods are used, including Broms, strain wedge and p-y analyses depending on structure and foundation (AASHTO 2014), p-y analyses being recommended. Displacements are analyzed at Service load conditions to stay below tolerable structure displacements, often limited by effects on the structure: closure of bridge joints, excessive lean or rotation, displacement of one element into another, aesthetics. The tolerable magnitude is set by the structural engineer and may be based on considerations other than the geotechnical or structural capacity of the foundation (often less than the elements can withstand, especially ductile steel piles). Limiting deflections are assessed with Service combinations and load and resistance factors of 1.0. Deformation analyses generally use p-y methods, or the strain wedge method or FEM (Chapter 6); displacements can also come from lateral load tests. Each element or group should meet the criteria for the structure (p. 45), checking horizontal movement at the top of the foundation, rotation at the top, horizontal movement under scour at the design flood, and horizontal displacement at the superstructure level. Lateral displacement may also define Geotechnical Strength Limit States (Chapter 5), and may matter for Extreme Events to keep adjacent structures from impacting each other or avoid excessive damage. Earthquakes can cause liquefaction or slope displacement; movement of a slope or of surficial blocks over a liquefied layer may displace foundations, add loads and reduce the deformation capacity left for the service limit. Field tests of drilled shafts and piles measuring lateral displacement are in Brown et al. (2010) (Figure 4-6). Measurements of deformation should be part of any lateral load test program and can be part of performance monitoring, e.g., inclinometers in slope stabilization shafts to verify stabilization or show the need for more elements; field testing and instrumentation are in Chapter 12. (pp. 44 to 45)
key_points: Tolerable lateral displacement is project specific and set by the structural engineer (p. 44).
Service: load and resistance factors 1.0; p-y analysis recommended (p. 44).
Tolerable values are often less than the elements can withstand, especially ductile steel piles (p. 44).
Check head movement, head rotation, movement under design-flood scour, superstructure displacement (p. 45).
Inclinometers in slope stabilization shafts verify performance (p. 45).

sections.applicability: Lateral displacement check for bridge foundations, retaining walls, and noise/sign structures at service loads

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit State
sections.summary: Extreme Event Limit States cover events with return periods longer than the design life: check flood (500-year scour), earthquakes and major vessel or vehicle collision. The aim is survival and life safety, accepting damage without collapse. The recommended resistance factor for geotechnical lateral resistance is 0.80 (Brown et al. 2010).
sections.body: Extreme Event Limit State failure modes relate to strength and stability under unique loading events with a return period greater than the bridge design life: check flood (500-year event for scour), earthquakes and/or major vessel or vehicle collision. The concern is survival of the bridge and protection of life safety, expecting some damage without collapse. The recommended load and resistance factor for extreme events is 0.80 for geotechnical lateral resistance (Brown et al. 2010); Chapter 8 discusses the Extreme Event Limit State in detail. (p. 46)
key_points: Events: check flood (500-year scour), earthquake, major vessel or vehicle collision (p. 46).
Goal: survival and life safety; damage accepted without collapse (p. 46).
Resistance factor 0.80 for geotechnical lateral resistance (Brown et al. 2010) (p. 46).
sections.applicability: Laterally loaded deep foundations subject to seismic, vessel collision, or 500-year scour loading

sections.title: Considerations for Limit Equilibrium Applications
sections.summary: Global stability of retaining structures and slope stabilization uses limit equilibrium, where current resistance and load factors are typically not applied. Software analyses use Strength I combinations, load factor 1.0 and resistance factor 0.75 (Strength load factors on supported structure foundation loads); use 0.65 where parameters and stratigraphy are highly variable or based on limited information.
sections.body: Global stability of retaining structures and slope stabilization needs limit equilibrium analyses. Resistance factors and additional load factors in current standards are typically not applied to loads and resistances in limit equilibrium analyses. In software, the analyses are performed at the Strength I load combinations, targeting a load factor of 1.0 and a resistance factor of 0.75. If a structure foundation is supported, 0.75 is used with Strength Limit load factors applied to the foundation loads, consistent with current Strength load groups and factors. A resistance factor of 0.65 should be used when the geotechnical parameters and stratigraphy are highly variable or based on limited information. Slope stabilization with deep foundations is discussed in Chapter 10. (p. 46)
key_points: Global stability: Strength I combinations, load factor 1.0, resistance factor 0.75 (p. 46).
Supporting a structure: 0.75 with Strength load factors on the foundation loads (p. 46).
Use 0.65 where parameters or stratigraphy are highly variable or based on limited information (p. 46).
sections.applicability: Global stability analysis for retaining walls and slope stabilization applications
